opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing to say is that SWE-bench has been really useful, and part of why it worked is that it was grounded in real issues from real repositories. But it captures a fairly narrow slice of what software engineers do: you're handed a well-scoped issue, you produce a patch, and a set of tests tells you whether you passed. Real engineering is much messier than that. You often have to figure out what the actual problem is, ask clarifying questions, make design decisions, and live with the consequences of those decisions over time.

So one direction I'd like to see is evaluations that are longer-horizon and more stateful. Instead of asking whether an agent can fix one issue, ask whether it can build and maintain a codebase over many iterations as the requirements change. A solution that passes today's tests but leaves behind a mess should score worse, because that mess makes the next change harder. Today's benchmarks mostly can't see that.

The second direction is moving beyond binary pass/fail. As tasks get more open-ended, there often isn't a single correct answer, so we need richer measures of quality: maintainability, efficiency, cost, and how reliable the agent is across repeated runs. If an agent succeeds six times out of ten, that's a very different product from one that succeeds ten out of ten, especially once you start chaining steps together, because those errors compound.

Third, I'd like evaluations to bring the human back into the picture. In practice, most of these systems are working with people, so it matters how well they handle underspecified instructions, whether they know when to ask for help, and how much of a person's time they actually save. A model might top a leaderboard and still create more review burden than it removes.

And finally, the evals need to keep moving. Once a benchmark becomes a target, people optimize for it, whether through overfitting or test contamination, and it gradually stops telling you much. So I'd like to see them refreshed continually with new tasks, and tied much more closely to real-world outcomes. Ultimately the question isn't "what's your score?" It's "can I trust this agent to do a meaningful piece of work on its own, and how would I know if it went wrong?" That's the bar evaluations should be helping us measure.

r001.rationale: Recommends longer-horizon, stateful evaluations that test building and maintaining a codebase over many iterations, beyond a single issue fix.

r002.rationale: Does not identify memory as a key challenge for long-horizon tasks.

r003.rationale: Mentions changing requirements, but does not identify continual learning as a key challenge.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I helped build SWE-bench, and I'm proud of it, but I'll be the first to say it's a snapshot of a very narrow slice of what we actually care about. It's a GitHub issue, a repository, and a set of hidden tests. The agent either makes the tests pass or it doesn't. That was a deliberate choice because it gave us something verifiable at scale, but it leaves out most of what real software engineering, and real work in general, looks like.

A few directions I'd like to see.

The first is moving from single-shot tasks to long-horizon, interactive ones. In the real world, nobody hands you a perfectly specified issue. You get an ambiguous request, you ask a clarifying question, the user changes their mind halfway through, the requirements turn out to be inconsistent with the codebase. I'd like evaluations where the agent has to work with a simulated user over many turns, and where part of what we score is whether it knew when to ask versus when to just proceed. Right now we mostly measure "did you solve it," and we're silent on "did you recognize that this task was underspecified."

Second, I want evaluations that measure the process, not just the outcome. A patch that passes the tests but deletes half the test suite, or hardcodes the expected output, is not a success. We've seen plenty of that. So things like: did the agent write its own tests, did it leave the codebase in a maintainable state, did it introduce regressions in functionality that wasn't covered by the hidden tests. That requires richer grading, probably some combination of execution, static analysis, and careful rubric-based judgment. It's harder, it's noisier, but it's closer to the thing we care about.

Third, and this is the one I'm most excited about, is evaluations in environments that are genuinely open-ended. SWE-bench is nice because the task is bounded by a repo. But a lot of valuable work is more like, here's a vague research question, go figure out what to do. Or here's a messy dataset and a goal, build the pipeline. There's no single hidden test. You have to judge the quality of the outcome the way a reviewer or a manager would. I think we're going to need to get comfortable with evaluations where the ground truth is a distribution of acceptable outcomes rather than a single answer, and where we use models themselves, carefully calibrated against human judgment, to do part of the grading.

And then there's the contamination and saturation problem, which is structural. Every static benchmark has a half-life. The moment it's popular, it ends up in training data, people start overfitting to its quirks, and the numbers stop meaning what they used to mean. So I'd like to see more evaluations that are living, that regenerate from fresh sources, real repositories, real issues filed after a cutoff, procedurally generated environments, so that the thing you're measuring stays honest.

If I had to compress it into one sentence: I want us to stop asking "can the model solve this puzzle" and start asking "would I trust this system as a colleague on a project that matters." That's a much harder question to operationalize, but it's the one that actually matters for how these systems get deployed.

r001.rationale: The response recommends moving beyond single-shot tasks to long-horizon, interactive evaluations spanning many turns.

r002.rationale: It does not identify memory as a challenge for long-horizon tasks.

r003.rationale: It does not identify continual learning as a challenge for long-horizon tasks.

astra-6.text:
I’d like to see evaluations move toward longer, more interactive tasks. Something like SWE-bench gives you a concrete problem and a way to check the result, which is useful. But in practice, figuring out what the problem is can be a big part of the work.

For example, if you ask an AI to build a piece of software, can it clarify your requirements, make a plan, test its assumptions, and adapt when you change your mind? Can it recognize when it needs your help? I’d want evaluations to capture that whole process, along with whether the final result actually meets your needs.

There’s also a question of reliability. Getting a task right once is different from consistently doing it well across slightly different situations. So I’d like us to measure how reliably these systems make progress over longer interactions, and how much human intervention they require.

r001.rationale: It recommends evaluations of “longer, more interactive tasks” and measuring progress over longer interactions, beyond a single bounded task.

r002.rationale: It does not identify memory as a challenge for long-horizon tasks.

r003.rationale: It mentions adapting when requirements change, but does not identify continual learning as a key challenge for long-horizon tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d like to see evaluations move toward longer, more open-ended tasks, where success isn’t just getting a patch to pass a set of tests. SWE-bench is useful because it grounds evaluation in real software problems, but it captures one slice of what we want these systems to do.

For example, can an AI take a vague goal, figure out what information it needs, ask useful questions, and work with a person to get to a good outcome? Can it recover when something goes wrong halfway through? Those capabilities are harder to capture with a single score, but they matter a lot in practice.

I’d also like evaluations to tell us more about why a system fails. Did it misunderstand the goal, make a bad plan, or fail to recognize that it needed help? If we can distinguish those things, evaluations become much more useful for improving the systems, rather than just ranking them.

r001.rationale: The response recommends longer, open-ended evaluations and contrasts them with a patch passing tests.

r002.rationale: It does not identify memory as a challenge for long-horizon tasks.

r003.rationale: It does not identify continual learning as a challenge for long-horizon tasks.
